client: I've been really struggling since last week when our team missed a major project deadline. I just took on this project manager role a few months ago, and now I feel like everyone is looking at me like I completely failed. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything — the deadline is still missed and my reputation at work might already be damaged.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling exposed and worried right now — stepping into a new role and then hitting a significant setback is genuinely hard, and those feelings of being watched and judged are really painful to carry. I also hear your skepticism about whether talking helps, and I want to gently offer that while it won't undo the missed deadline, it might help us untangle what's fact versus what your mind is filling in about how others see you. When you say your reputation "might already be damaged," I'm curious — what specific evidence have you actually seen from your colleagues, versus what you're imagining or predicting might be true?

client: Honestly, when I try to separate what I've actually seen versus what I'm imagining, I realize most of it is in my head — no one has said anything directly to me, and my manager just sent a pretty neutral follow-up email. But that almost makes it worse, because the silence feels like people are talking about me behind my back rather than to my face, and I keep reading into every small interaction like when a colleague didn't say good morning today. I know that probably sounds irrational, but it's hard to just switch off that feeling that something is off.
therapist: It doesn't sound irrational at all — your mind is trying to protect you by scanning for danger signals, which is a very human response to feeling vulnerable in a new role. What's worth noticing, though, is that you just did something really skillful: you caught yourself interpreting silence and a missed "good morning" as confirmation of something that hasn't actually been stated, which in CBT we'd call "mind reading." What do you think might be some other, equally plausible explanations for your colleague not saying good morning today?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess logically I can come up with other explanations — maybe she was just distracted, or running late, or had something on her mind that had nothing to do with me. But the thing is, even when I tell myself that, it doesn't really make the feeling go away, you know? It still sits in my chest like this low-level dread that I'm somehow already failing at this job and people are starting to notice.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that knowing something logically and *feeling* it emotionally are two different things, and that gap can be genuinely frustrating. That "dread in your chest" sounds like it might be connected to a deeper belief, something like "I'm not good enough for this role," which no amount of rational counter-arguments will fully quiet on its own. I'm wondering — is this feeling of being on the verge of being "found out" something that's shown up for you before in your life, or does it feel specific to this new role?

client: Yeah, it's definitely not new. I remember feeling this way back in college too, like I'd somehow tricked my professors into thinking I was smarter than I actually was, and eventually they'd figure it out. It's just... exhausting carrying that around, and honestly kind of lonely, because I can't exactly tell my coworkers "hey, I think I'm a fraud" without it becoming a whole thing.
therapist: What you're describing — that persistent sense of being one step away from being "found out" — has a name, impostor syndrome, and I want you to know it's remarkably common among capable, conscientious people, which actually tells us something important: it tends to follow achievement, not failure. The loneliness you're feeling makes so much sense when you're carrying a secret that feels too risky to share, and it can make the burden so much heavier than it needs to be. I'm curious — when you look back at your college experience, do you think your professors were actually tricked, or is it possible their positive view of you was simply... accurate?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but then I think... they only saw what I showed them. Like, I was really good at asking the right questions and sounding like I understood things, but half the time I was just piecing it together as I went. It doesn't feel like the same thing as actually being smart, even if the grades said otherwise.
therapist: What you just described — asking good questions, piecing things together under pressure, figuring it out as you go — that actually *is* what competence looks like in practice, not a performance of it; very few people, even experts, operate from a place of complete certainty. It's worth gently challenging the idea that there's some "real" version of being smart that you're falling short of, when what you're describing sounds a lot like exactly the kind of adaptive, resourceful thinking that makes someone effective in a project manager role. I'm curious — if a colleague described their own working style the way you just described yours, would you see them as a fraud, or would you see someone who was doing their job well?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't call a colleague a fraud for that. I'd probably think they were handling things pretty well, actually. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to hold myself to a higher standard, or like I'm the only one who knows how much I'm winging it.
therapist: You just caught something really significant — you're applying two completely different standards, one generous and realistic for others, and one harsh and almost impossible for yourself, and that double standard is worth examining because it's not based on evidence, it's based on a rule you've quietly imposed on yourself. That sense of "I'm the only one who knows how much I'm winging it" is actually something most people around you are probably feeling too, just as privately and silently as you are. What do you think that harsher standard for yourself is protecting you from, or what do you imagine might happen if you let yourself be held to the same fair standard you'd apply to a colleague?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... if I let myself off the hook the way I would with a colleague, maybe I'd stop trying as hard, like the harsh standard is the only thing keeping me from completely falling apart or being exposed as someone who doesn't belong here. But even as I say that out loud, I can hear how exhausting that sounds, and I'm not sure the fear is actually based on anything real.
therapist: You just did something really courageous — you named the hidden logic behind the harsh inner critic, that it feels like a necessary engine keeping you going, and then in the same breath you questioned whether it's actually true. What's worth sitting with is that you've achieved real things, navigated a new role, recognized your own patterns, shown up even when it's hard — not *because* of the fear, but possibly *in spite* of how much energy it drains from you. I wonder, what might it look like to stay motivated and conscientious in your work, but fueled by something gentler than the constant threat of being "found out"?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it's possible, but I honestly don't know what that gentler fuel would even feel like. Like, fear and self-criticism are so familiar at this point that they almost feel like the only things I know how to run on. If I let go of that constant pressure, I'm genuinely afraid I'd just... stop caring, or stop trying altogether.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — when something has been your primary coping engine for so long, it's genuinely hard to imagine functioning without it, almost like being afraid to let go of a life raft even when you're already close to shore. But I'd gently offer that the fact you're here, reflecting this honestly and caring this deeply about your work and how others see you, suggests that your drive comes from something real inside you — not just from fear. I'm curious, can you think of even one small moment in your work or life where you felt motivated by something other than fear — maybe curiosity, pride, or genuine interest — even briefly?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, it's always been fear driving me. But... there was this one project last year where I got so absorbed in solving a design problem that I genuinely forgot to check if my boss had responded to my email, which is basically unheard of for me. I don't know if that counts, but it felt different — lighter somehow, like I was doing it because I actually wanted to figure it out, not because I was terrified of getting it wrong.
therapist: That absolutely counts — and the way you described it, "lighter," absorbed, genuinely wanting to figure it out, is actually a beautiful example of what intrinsic motivation feels like, and it was already inside you, not something you need to build from scratch. What's really meaningful is that you accessed it naturally, without needing fear to push you there, which tells us the harsh inner critic isn't the source of your capability — it's just been taking credit for it. I'm wondering, what was it about that particular problem that pulled you in so completely, and is there anything about your current role that has even a small trace of that same quality?

client: That's an interesting question, and honestly it's making me sit with something uncomfortable. The puzzle that pulled me in was completely open-ended, no one was grading me or waiting on me, so I think the freedom from judgment is what made it feel safe to just... explore. My current role has almost none of that, everything I do gets reviewed and evaluated, so even when a problem is technically interesting, that weight of being watched kind of kills the natural curiosity before it can breathe.
therapist: You've just made a really insightful connection — that it's not curiosity that's missing, it's the psychological safety to let it breathe, and the constant evaluation in your role is triggering that same "being watched" feeling that feeds the impostor syndrome. What's worth noticing is that the judgment you're most afraid of may actually be your own — your inner critic is often the loudest evaluator in the room, even before anyone else weighs in. I'm wondering, if you could carve out even one small part of your workday that you mentally framed as "exploration space" rather than "performance space," what might that look like for you?
